--- title: "Additional Analyses" format: html: toc: true toc-depth: 3 code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" --- In what follows, please find the results of additional analyses: variance inflation factors, the originally preregistered model, results without covariates, results with all participants (hence, including those removed due to speeding or response patterns), and frequentist robustness and moderation analyses. For the main analyses, see [Analyses](05a_analyses.html). All analyses on this page focus on communication (the number of words), the main outcome of the study. Self-disclosure is only analyzed in the main analyses, because it is addressed in one additional research question (RQ2). # Setup Load packages. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # define packages packages <- c("cowplot", "devtools", "faoutlier", "GGally", "kableExtra", "knitr", "lavaan", "magrittr", "MVN", "psych", "pwr", "quanteda", "semTools", "td", "tidyverse") # load packages lapply(packages, library, character.only = TRUE, quietly = TRUE) ``` ::: Load data. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load workspace (created in the main analyses) load("data/workspace.RData") # originally preregistered outcome: words + reactions (likes/dislikes count twice), log-transformed d$words_react_log <- log1p(d$words + 2 * d$reactions) ``` ::: # Variance Inflation Factors In what follows, you can find estimations of variance inflation factors, which help gauge multicollinearity. Generally, values above 5 or even 10 are considered problematic. However, these are only rules of thumb, and multicollinearity can occur with lower values. Indeed, although the values reported below are not above 5, they are increased, suggesting that multicollinearity might be at play here, which the preregistered analyses also confirm. Each variable is regressed on all other privacy calculus variables (controlling for gender, age, and education). The VIF is then computed from the explained variance: VIF = 1 / (1 − R²). When comparing the analyses, the results do not differ in any meaningful way. # Frequentist Robustness and Moderation Analyses In what follows, we report frequentist robustness checks of the main analyses (see [Analyses](05a_analyses.html)). These models are easier to interpret than the Bayesian hurdle models. As in the paper, the main focus is on communication. We estimate three types of models: 1. **Logistic regressions:** Did participants communicate at all? 2. **OLS regressions** with the log-transformed number of words: How much did participants communicate? 3. **Negative binomial regressions** with the raw number of words: How much did participants communicate? These models account for the count nature and the skewness of the data. For each predictor, we also test whether its effect depends on the popularity cues (moderation). The first model of each type includes the predictor and the experimental condition, the second model adds their interaction, and the third model additionally controls for gender, age, and education. All privacy calculus variables are mean scores on the original 1–7 scale (not standardized). They use the same items as in the main analyses, including general trust. As an additional check, we analyze a second outcome: communication including reactions (the number of words plus twice the number of likes and dislikes given). This was the outcome of the original preregistration. Note that it is *not* the self-disclosure index of the main analyses. ## Setup The following models are fast. We therefore turn off caching and code reformatting. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} knitr::opts_chunk$set(cache = FALSE, tidy = FALSE) ``` ::: Load the packages. The package `conflicted` makes sure that functions with the same name in different packages (e.g., `select()` in dplyr and MASS) are not mixed up. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} options(repos = c(CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org")) packages <- c("tidyverse", "texreg", "marginaleffects", "ggpubr", "MASS", "DescTools", "conflicted") # install missing packages, then load all load_p <- function(){ for (p in packages) { if (!requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)) { install.packages(p) } library(p, character.only = TRUE) } } load_p() # resolve conflicts between packages conflict_scout() conflicts_prefer(dplyr::select) conflicts_prefer(dplyr::filter) ``` ::: Load the data, as saved at the end of the main analyses (final sample). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- readr::read_csv("data/data.csv") ``` ::: Compute the privacy calculus variables as mean scores. We use the same items as in the main analyses (e.g., without the deleted items, and general trust). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- data |> rowwise() |> mutate( self_eff = mean(c_across(SE01_01:SE01_04), na.rm = TRUE), pri_con = mean(c_across(c(PC01_01, PC01_02, PC01_04:PC01_07)), na.rm = TRUE), grats_gen = mean(c_across(GR02_01:GR02_05), na.rm = TRUE), pri_delib = mean(c_across(PD01_01:PD01_05), na.rm = TRUE), # general trust in the provider, the website, and the other users (as in the main analyses) trust_gen = mean(c_across(TR02_01:TR02_03), na.rm = TRUE) ) |> ungroup() ``` ::: Compute the outcomes: whether participants communicated at all, and the second outcome (words + reactions). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- data |> mutate( # did participants communicate at all?
